newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds charge higher on EMU convergence trade.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds charge higher on EMU convergence trade.

text.p: Irish government bonds charged upwards in frenetic trade on Friday, spurred on by heavy foreign buying on the back of EMU convergence expectations, dealers said.
The spread against Bunds in the 10-year area of the curve fell to a new low level of around 90 basis points, after spending the week flirting with the 100-basis-points level.
Dealers said foreign investors had been buying the market on the expectation that Irish and German yields would converge as EMU (Economic and Monetary Union) approaches.
"The market is really roaring ahead today. We have seen a lot of foreign cash coming into the market," one dealer said.

Dealers said the Irish market had been strong all week after last weekend's informal meeting of European Union finance ministers in Dublin raised expectations that EMU would take place on time. The strength of the Irish pound against the mark was also inspiring convergence plays in bonds, they said.

The Irish currency was perched at the top of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) grid at 1040 GMT. The eight percent bond due 2000 was up 60p at 106.00 to yield 6.19 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 55p at 107.15, yielding 6.85.
Padhraic Garvey, senior economist at Riada Stockbrokers, said the 10-year spread was likely to stabilise at around 90 basis points over Germany over the next few months.
"We hit 90 basis points today. The question is whether it's sustainable. In the short term it certainly is, although of course you have to allow for setbacks along the way," he said,

"But given that we're very serious EMU candidates, you've got to pencil in a convergence to Bunds in the years leading up to EMU. We see 75 basis points on a sustainable basis next year and 50 basis points the following year, with a view to seeing spreads about 25 over Bunds within EMU," Garvey said.
He said that over the next few months, spreads might move closer to Bunds but would tend to gravitate back to around 90 basis points.

The market could also be vulnerable to short-term setbacks, Garvey said. "The punt could fall against the mark, and you always have to watch Irish credit numbers, which are out next week," he said. In recent months high Irish credit growth has spooked the domestic bond market.
"If foreigners feel the market has stalled we could see them taking profits on a large-scale basis," he added. "But at the moment there's no obvious problem around the corner."
